name: Brahui
confidence_why: Bray 1909, Emeneau 1937, Andronov 1980 and Elfenbein 1998 all describe the same weak, non-contrastive stress that sits on the first syllable of the word unless a long vowel draws it, and the only different wording, Krishnamurti 2003's family-wide "initial syllable, short or long", is a survey generalization about Dravidian as a whole that still grants a non-initial long vowel is louder.

new_statements.quote: Stress, while audible, is not phonemic in Brahui. Long vowels attract stress; where more than one long vowel occurs in a word, the first one is stressed. Poly-syllabic words with no long vowels are generally stressed on the first syllable. For further discussion of Brahui phonology, the reader is referred to Elfenbein (1997) and DeArmond (1975). [p. 394] ... short vowels contrast with long vowels, but only in the first syllable. Pho-netically stressed, phonemically long vowels /i e o u/ have higher tongue posi-tions than the corresponding unstressed short vowels. Stressed and long /a/ = [a:] is lower and more central than its corresponding short unstressed /a/ = [a]. [p. 391; scanned, macrons lost]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is audible but not phonemic. The leftmost long-vowel syllable carries the stress; if the word has no long vowel, stress is generally on the first syllable. (Since long vowels contrast with short only in the first syllable per p. 391, the two clauses usually coincide on the initial syllable; the long-vowel clause matters for loans and polysyllables with non-initial long vowels.)
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for Brahui (the volume's secondary-stress sentence retrieved by the same search belongs to the Konda chapter, p. 245).
new_statements.exceptions: 'generally' stressed on the first syllable when no long vowel is present (no explicit exceptions listed); stress conditions vowel quality (stressed long e/o open, unstressed closed; stressed long a lower and more central). The index also lists a stress mention on p. 400 (morphology) that the full-text-search highlight cap did not surface.
new_statements.identity_note: Elfenbein 1998 describes Brahui in general (Kalat standard), noting only a northeastern free variation in aspiration; his Iranica article says the language is essentially without important dialectal variation (Sarawan/Jahlawan differ in /h/). Note that the listed open copy for work 0 is the Encyclopaedia Iranica 'BRAHUI' article (Elfenbein 1989, IV/4: 433-443), not the Routledge chapter; the listed open copy for work 1 is a one-page ERIC abstract card, not Krishnamurti's book.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide statement (Brahui is one of the 26 languages covered but is not singled out): stress is never phonemic in Dravidian; it normally falls on the first syllable whether short or long, while a non-initial long vowel is louder than short vowels.

readall_conflicts: No contradiction of type: every source read says Brahui stress is audible but not phonemic/contrastive. The placement statements differ in specificity rather than direction. Elfenbein 1998 (p. 394) gives a weight rule: the first long vowel of the word takes the stress, and only words with no long vowel default to the first syllable. Krishnamurti 2003 (p. 27, family-wide, not Brahui-specific) says stress normally falls on the initial syllable 'short or long' and describes a non-initial long vowel only as 'louder'; whether that counts as the word stress is left open, so the two are compatible but not identical. The sources already held by the project from the earlier reading line up with Elfenbein: Emeneau 1937 (BSOS 8: 981) says all polysyllabic words quoted have a stress accent on the first syllable except [ka?e:k], accented on its second (long-vowel) syllable; Campbell's compendium (Rosetta brh phon-1) says stress is weak, tending towards the beginning of the word; Syed et al. (Phonetica) say neither Brahui nor Balochi has contrastive lexical stress. The Encyclopaedia Iranica article (Elfenbein 1989) is silent on stress.

audit.recode_to: Conditional only: if Elfenbein 1997 states categorically 'stress on the first long vowel/diphthong, otherwise on the first syllable' without geminate/cluster attraction or hedges, kind would move from weight-hedged to unhedged quantity-sensitive (unbounded, leftmost heavy else leftmost/initial) with what counts as heavy: CVV rather than CVV+CVC; keep Bray sec. 203 / Bashir verb-form shifts as lexical-morphological exceptions.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: all three deciding passages are verbatim in the scanned files we hold at the stated djvu line locators (Bray sec. 11 lines 1703-1709, sec. 203 lines 7340ff; Andronov 1980 lines 76-91); only trivial scanned normalizations. (2) The classification rests on the standard reference grammar (Bray 1909, 242 pp) plus an independent Soviet grammar (Andronov 1980), which agree; open-text grade is honest. But Glottolog lists a dedicated phonology (Elfenbein 1997, 797-811) and a 1998 Routledge sketch that we do not hold, and two open secondary sources downloaded today (Syed et al. 2022 Phonetica, citing Elfenbein 1997b; Wikipedia citing Krishnamurti 2003) attribute to that literature a crisper, unhedged rule (long vowel, else first syllable) with no mention of geminate-closed syllables. That could shift 'weight-hedged' to plain quantity-sensitive and narrow the heavy class, so the record is adequate rather than well-sour
